claim: Hippocampal oscillations are dynamic, with unique oscillatory frequencies present during different behavioral states.
source: Hippocampal oscillations are dynamic, with unique oscillatory frequencies present during different behavioral states.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's premise.

claim: Single cell and local field potential activity were recorded from the CA1 region of the hippocampus as rats performed a context-guided odor-reward association task.
source: we recorded single cell and local field potential activity from the CA1 region of the hippocampus as rats performed a context-guided odor-reward association task.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Theta (4–12 Hz), beta (15–35 Hz), low gamma (35–55 Hz), and high gamma (65–90 Hz) frequencies exhibited dynamic amplitude profiles as rats sampled odor cues.
source: We found that theta (4–12 Hz), beta (15–35 Hz), low gamma (35–55 Hz), and high gamma (65–90 Hz) frequencies exhibited dynamic amplitude profiles as rats sampled odor cues.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Interneurons and principal cells exhibited unique engagement in each of the four rhythmic circuits in a manner that related to successful performance of the task.
source: Interneurons and principal cells exhibited unique engagement in each of the four rhythmic circuits in a manner that related to successful performance of the task.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2-5.

claim: Principal cells coherent to each rhythm differentially represented task dimensions.
source: Moreover, principal cells coherent to each rhythm differentially represented task dimensions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Distinct processing states arise from the engagement of rhythmically identifiable circuits, which have unique roles in organizing task-relevant processing in the hippocampus.
source: These results demonstrate that distinct processing states arise from the engagement of rhythmically identifiable circuits, which have unique roles in organizing task-relevant processing in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Neural oscillations arise from the temporal coordination of activity in organized networks of neurons.
source: Neural oscillations arise from the temporal coordination of activity in organized networks of neurons (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The unique connectivity of a network constrains the number of distinct rhythmic profiles that its local circuits can manifest.
source: The unique connectivity of a network constrains the number of distinct rhythmic profiles that its local circuits can manifest, and the input to the network at a given time dictates the rhythmic circuits that are engaged (Cannon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Changes in the oscillatory activity of the hippocampus occur as it processes information it receives from multiple brain regions.
source: Changes in the oscillatory activity of the hippocampus, a brain structure important for memory function, occur as it processes information it receives from multiple brain regions (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Cannon et al., 2014; Colgin et al., 2009; Schomburg, et al., 2014; Lee et al., 1994; Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The theta (4–12 Hz) rhythm is a dominant rhythm in the hippocampus that engages both principal and interneuron cell types.
source: The theta (4–12 Hz) rhythm is a dominant rhythm in the hippocampus that engages both principal and interneuron cell types, and depends on inputs from the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) and the medial septum (Lee et al., 1994; Buzsáki, 2002; Kocsis et al., 1999; Montgomery et al., 2009; Kubie et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The hippocampus exhibits oscillations in the beta and gamma frequency ranges that span from 15-150Hz.
source: The hippocampus also exhibits oscillations in the beta and gamma frequency ranges that span from 15-150Hz (Buzsáki and Freeman, 2015; Colgin and Moser, 2010; Kay and Freeman, 1998; Martin et al., 2007; Gourevitch et al., 2010; Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Slow and fast gamma oscillations in the CA1 region of the hippocampus are thought to arise from the influence of CA3 and MEC inputs, respectively.
source: Specifically, slow and fast gamma oscillations in the CA1 region of the hippocampus are thought to arise from the influence of CA3 and MEC inputs, respectively (Colgin et al., 2009; Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An intermediate beta frequency range in CA1 has been hypothesized to reflect inputs from the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC).
source: In addition, an intermediate beta frequency range in CA1 has been hypothesized to reflect inputs from the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A total of 1368 cells (1301 principal cells, 67 interneurons) were recorded from 6 rats across a total of 45 sessions.
source: We recorded a total of 1368 cells (1301 principal cells, 67 interneurons) from 6 rats across a total of 45 sessions.
evidence: This describes the dataset collected in the study.

claim: Prominent changes in amplitude were observed in the theta (4–12 Hz), beta (15–35 Hz), low gamma (35–55 Hz), and high gamma (65–90 Hz) frequency ranges during the nose poke interval.
source: Prominent changes in amplitude were observed in the theta (4–12 Hz), beta (15–35 Hz), low gamma (35–55 Hz), and high gamma (65–90 Hz) frequency ranges (Figure 1a (middle, bottom), b-c).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1.

claim: All four frequencies demonstrated significant changes in amplitude over the course of the nose poke.
source: We performed a two-factor repeated measures ANOVA and found a significant main effect of time during the nose poke for all frequencies (Figure 1e–h; time: repeated measures ANOVAtheta: d.f. = 5, F= 10.32, p<0.00001; repeated measures ANOVAbeta: d.f. = 5, F= 23.87, p<0.00001; repeated measures ANOVAlow gamma: d.f. = 5, F= 17.34, p<0.00001; repeated measures ANOVAhigh gamma: d.f. = 5, F= 63.78, p<0.00001)
evidence: Statistical analysis of amplitude changes over time is reported with specific test results.

claim: Mean amplitudes were not significantly different across correct and incorrect trial types for any frequency.
source: and no main effect for outcome (correct or incorrect) in any frequency (outcome: repeated measures ANOVAtheta: d.f. = 1, F= 1.19, p=0.2797, n.s.; repeated measures ANOVAbeta: d.f. = 1, F ≈ 0, p=0.9746, n.s.; repeated measures ANOVAlow gamma: d.f. = 1, F = 1.32, p=0.2546, n.s.; repeated measures ANOVAhigh gamma: d.f. = 1, F = 0.08, p=0.7747, n.s.).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows no main effect of trial outcome on amplitude.

claim: A significant interaction effect was observed in the low gamma35-55Hz frequency range, due to increased low gamma35-55Hz amplitude during correct trials during the last second of the odor-sampling interval.
source: However, we observed a significant interaction effect in the low gamma35-55Hz frequency range, due to increased low gamma35-55Hz amplitude during correct trials during the last second of the odor-sampling interval (time x outcome: repeated measures ANOVAtheta: d.f. = 5, F= 0.34, p=0.8886, n.s.; repeated measures ANOVAbeta: d.f. = 5, F = 1.46, p=0.2008, n.s.; repeated measures ANOVAlow gamma: d.f. = 5, F = 4.32, p=0.0008; repeated measures ANOVAhigh gamma: d.f. = 5, F = 0.40, p=0.8513, n.s.).
evidence: Statistical analysis reveals a significant interaction effect for low gamma amplitude.

claim: Of the interneurons that exhibited significant spike-phase coherence to beta15-35Hz, the number that exhibited coherence to beta15-35Hz during Correct Trials Only was greater than the numbers coherent during Incorrect Trials Only or All Trials.
source: Of the interneurons that exhibited significant spike-phase coherence to beta15-35Hz (Figure 2a, middle left), the number that exhibited coherence to beta15-35Hz during Correct Trials Only was greater than the numbers coherent during Incorrect Trials Only or All Trials (χ2beta (2, N=66) = 51.54, p<0.00001; post hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni adjusted alpha: χ2correct v incorrect (1, N=53) = 38.21, p<0.00001; χ2correct v all (1, N=62) = 20.90, p<0.00001; χ2incorrect v all (1, N=17) = 4.77, p=0.029, n.s.).
evidence: Statistical analysis of interneuron coherence patterns with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The largest number of theta4-12Hz coherent interneurons were coherent during All Trials.
source: In contrast, the largest number of theta4-12Hz coherent interneurons (Figure 2a, far left) were coherent during All Trials, although a greater number of cells still exhibited coherence during Correct Trials Only compared to Incorrect Trials Only (χ2theta (2, N=126) = 80.19, p<0.00001, post hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni adjusted alpha: χ2correct v incorrect (1, N=42) = 34.38, p<0.00001; χ2correct v all (1, N=124) = 15.61, p=0.00007; χ2incorrect v all (1, N=86) = 78.19, p<0.00001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of theta coherent interneurons with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Interneurons exhibited significantly higher firing rates during incorrect trials than correct trials.
source: To the contrary, we observed that interneurons exhibited significantly higher firing rates during incorrect trials than correct trials (Figure 3c; Mdncorrect = 12.78 Hz, Mdnincorrect = 14.20 Hz, Wilcoxon signed-rank test Z = -3.22, p=0.0013).
evidence: Statistical comparison of firing rates between trial types with reference to Figure 3c.

claim: For all rhythms, principal cells preferentially exhibited significant spike-phase coherence during Correct Trials Only.
source: For all rhythms, principal cells preferentially exhibited significant spike-phase coherence during Correct Trials Only (theta: χ2theta (2, N=349) = 266.86, p<0.00001, post hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni adjusted alpha: χ2correct v incorrect (1, N=298) = 165.38, p<0.00001; χ2correct v all (1, N=311) = 140.45, p<0.00001; χ2incorrect v all (1, N=89) = 1.90, p=0.1682, n.s.; beta: χ2beta (2, N=91) = 92.40, p<0.00001, post hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni adjusted alpha: χ2correct v incorrect (1, N=88) =38.23, p<0.00001; χ2correct v all (1, N=76) = 64.47, p<0.00001; χ2incorrect v all (1, N=18) = 8.00, p=0.0047; low gamma: χ2low gamma (2, N=120) = 132.65, p<0.00001, post hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni adjusted alpha: χ2correct v incorrect (1, N=116) = 57.97, p<0.00001; χ2correct v all (1, N=101) = 85.63, p<0.00001; χ2incorrect v all (1, N=21) = 8.05, p=0.0045; high gamma: χ2high gamma (2, N=134) = 132.65, p<0.00001, post hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni adjusted alpha: χ2correct v incorrect (1, N=128) = 66.13, p<0.00001; χ2correct v all (1, N=116) = 93.24, p<0.00001; χ2incorrect v all (1, N=24) = 6.00, p=0.0143).
evidence: Statistical analysis of principal cell coherence patterns across all rhythms.

claim: Principal cells exhibited no significant differences in firing rates between correct and incorrect trials.
source: To ensure that these changes in coherence strength were not due to decreases in principal cell firing rates during incorrect trials, we compared the firing rates across trial types and found no significant differences between correct and incorrect trials (Figure 4c; Mdncorrect = 0.6000 Hz, Mdnincorrect = 0.4444 Hz, Wilcoxon signed-rank test = 0.5608, p=0.5750).
evidence: Statistical comparison of principal cell firing rates with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: Interneurons were significantly more engaged in multiple rhythms than the principal cell population in each rhythmic category.
source: Tests for differences between the interneuron and principal cell populations revealed that interneurons were significantly more engaged in multiple rhythms than the principal cell population in each rhythmic category (χ2theta (P v I) (1, N=300) = 49.65, p<0.00001; χ2beta (P v I) (1, N=122) = 33.40, p<0.00001; χ2low gamma (P v I) (1, N=145) = 26.56, p<0.00001; χ2high gamma (P v I) (1, N=178) = 31.17, p<0.00001; for the interneurons and principal cells engaged in multiple rhythms, see the specific combination of rhythms in Figure 2—source data 1 and 2, respectively).
evidence: Statistical comparison between interneurons and principal cells regarding multi-rhythm engagement.

claim: Interneurons were not equally distributed across the fifteen combinations of the four rhythms during correct trials.
source: Interneurons were not equally distributed across the fifteen combinations of the four rhythms during correct trials (χ2correct (14, N=134) = 326.97, p<0.00001), with the largest number of the interneurons coherent to all four rhythms.
evidence: Statistical analysis of interneuron distribution across rhythm combinations.

claim: During incorrect trials, interneurons were most often coherent to theta4-12 Hz only.
source: In contrast, during incorrect trials, the interneurons were unequally distributed such that they were most often coherent to theta4-12 Hz only (χ2incorrect (14, N=100) = 203.30, p<0.00001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of interneuron distribution during incorrect trials.

claim: Theta4-12 Hz and low gamma35-55 Hz amplitudes are more anti-correlated than all other pairs of frequencies.
source: Specifically, theta4-12 Hz and low gamma35-55 Hz amplitudes are more anti-correlated than all other pairs of frequencies (Tukey's Honest Significant Difference test, p<0.00001, for all post hoc pairwise comparisons of theta4-12 Hz and low gamma35-55 Hz amplitude correlations against all other pairs of frequencies).
evidence: Statistical analysis of amplitude correlations between frequency pairs.

claim: Theta4-12 Hz coherent cells exhibited increases in information for each task dimension across the three intervals examined.
source: Theta4-12 Hz coherent cells exhibited increases in information for each task dimension across the three intervals examined (Figure 6c–e, position: Friedman's testtheta: d.f. = 2, χ2 = 47.19, p<0.00001; odor: Friedman's testtheta: d.f. = 2, χ2 = 15.89, p=0.0004; odor-position: Friedman's testtheta: d.f. = 2, χ2 = 31.54, p<0.00001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of information content in theta coherent cells with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Beta15-35 Hz coherent cells exhibited significant increases in information only for odor-position conjunctions, and only at the end of the poke.
source: In contrast, beta15-35 Hz coherent cells exhibited significant increases in information only for odor-position conjunctions, and only at the end of the poke, when the rat had committed to a decision (position: Friedman's testbeta: d.f. = 2, χ2 = 5.78, p=0.0556; odor: Friedman's testbeta: d.f. = 2, χ2 = 2.96, p=0.2275; odor-position: Friedman's testbeta: d.f. = 2, χ2 = 6.56, p=0.0376).
evidence: Statistical analysis of information content in beta coherent cells.

claim: Principal cell and interneuron entrainment to beta15-35Hz frequency oscillations were the most correlated with correct performance.
source: Notably, principal cell and interneuron entrainment to beta15-35Hz frequency oscillations were the most correlated with correct performance.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Introduction section.

claim: The beta15-35Hz rhythm instigates a processing of information in the hippocampus that is distinct from the processing that occurs in theta4-12Hz, low gamma35-55Hz, and high gamma65-90Hz.
source: We propose that the beta15-35Hz rhythm instigates a processing of information in the hippocampus that is distinct from the processing that occurs in theta4-12Hz, low gamma35-55Hz, and high gamma65-90Hz and that the presence of the beta15-35Hz rhythm signals a recruitment of cell activity that may be critical for memory function.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation stated in the Introduction.

claim: Rats learned that pairs of odors have differential value (rewarded or unrewarded) depending upon the spatial context in which they are presented.
source: In our task, rats learned that pairs of odors have differential value (rewarded or unrewarded) depending upon the spatial context in which they are presented (Figure 1a (top), see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task design.

claim: The initiation of a poke triggered the release of an odor after a 250 ms delay.
source: The initiation of a poke triggered the release of an odor after a 250 ms delay.
evidence: This describes a specific timing parameter of the behavioral task.

claim: Neural activity was analyzed during trials when the rat maintained a nose poke for 1.5 s while sampling a rewarded odor (correct trials) and during trials when the rat maintained a nose poke for 1.5 s while sampling the non-rewarded odor (incorrect trials).
source: We analyzed neural activity during trials when the rat maintained a nose poke for 1.5 s while sampling a rewarded odor (correct trials) and during trials when the rat maintained a nose poke for 1.5 s while sampling the non-rewarded odor (incorrect trials).
evidence: This describes the trial types analyzed in the study.

claim: The diffuse, local projections of the interneuron population place them in an ideal position to shape the rhythmic organization of the network in response to inputs received from a diverse array of afferents.
source: The diffuse, local projections of the interneuron population place them in an ideal position to shape the rhythmic organization of the network in response to inputs received from a diverse array of afferents (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996; Sik et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Interneurons in the CA1 region differ greatly according to their thresholds of excitability, the decay time of their inhibition, and the subcellular compartments where they preferentially target principal cells.
source: Interneurons in the CA1 region differ greatly according to their thresholds of excitability, the decay time of their inhibition, and the subcellular compartments where they preferentially target principal cells (Cannon et al., 2014; Royer et al., 2012; Roux et al., 2014; Roux and Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transient increases in the amplitude of higher frequency beta and low gamma activity can be observed during the presentation of conditioned stimuli.
source: Transient increases in the amplitude of higher frequency beta and low gamma activity can be observed during the presentation of conditioned stimuli, suggesting that the hippocampus undergoes a change in processing state (Igarashi et al., 2014; Kay and Freeman, 1998; Gourevitch et al., 2010; Berke et al., 2008; Rangel et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cross-frequency coupling in the hippocampus develops while learning context-guided odor-reward associations.
source: In addition, cross-frequency coupling in the hippocampus develops while learning context-guided odor-reward associations (Tort et al., 2009; 2010), which occurs concurrently with the development of odor-place conjunctive encoding in hippocampal principal neurons (Komorowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Single neurons in the CA3 and CA1 regions of the hippocampus develop activity that is selective for odors, odor port locations, and conjunctions of particular odors at specific locations (odor-position selectivity).
source: In previous studies, it has been shown that single neurons in the CA3 and CA1 regions of the hippocampus develop activity that is selective for odors, odor port locations, and conjunctions of particular odors at specific locations (odor-position selectivity) (Komorowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The nose poke interval contains a shift in processing state in the hippocampus, which is observable through the onset of changes in rhythmic circuits.
source: Together, these results indicate that the nose poke interval contains a shift in processing state in the hippocampus, which is observable through the onset of changes in rhythmic circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amplitude dynamics results.

claim: Interneurons that exhibited significant spike-phase coherence to theta4-12Hz, beta15-35Hz, and high gamma65-90Hz during Correct Trials Only did not exhibit a consistent phase preference between correct and incorrect trials.
source: Interneurons that were coherent to theta4-12Hz, beta15-35Hz, and high gamma65-90Hz during Correct Trials Only did not exhibit a consistent phase preference between correct and incorrect trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c; Rtheta-correct = 0.26, p=0.0823; Rbeta-correct = 0.12, p=0.4003; Rhigh gamma-correct = 0.16, p=0.2012).
evidence: Statistical analysis of phase preferences with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Interneurons that were coherent to theta4-12Hz, beta15-35Hz, low gamma35-55Hz, and high gamma65-90Hz during All Trials exhibited relatively strong correlations between the average phases observed across the population during correct and incorrect trials.
source: In stark contrast, interneurons that were coherent to theta4-12Hz, beta15-35Hz, low gamma35-55Hz, and high gamma65-90Hz during All Trials exhibited relatively strong correlations between the average phases observed across the population during correct and incorrect trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d; Rtheta-all = 0.82, p<0.00001; Rbeta-all = 0.55, p=0.0402; Rlow gamma-all = 0.41, p=0.0131; Rhigh gamma-all = 0.66, p=0.0002).
evidence: Statistical analysis of phase correlations with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The principal cells coherent to theta4-12 Hz, beta15-35 Hz, and high gamma65-90 Hz during Correct Trials Only did not exhibit a consistent phase preference across correct and incorrect trial types.
source: The principal cells coherent to theta4-12 Hz and high gamma65-90 Hz during Correct Trials Only did not exhibit a consistent phase preference across correct and incorrect trial types (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c; Rtheta-correct = -0.05, p=0.4107; Rhigh gamma-correct = -0.10, p=0.2239)
evidence: Statistical analysis of phase preferences with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: For the principal cells coherent to beta15-35 Hz during Correct Trials Only, the preferred phase during correct trials was anti-correlated to the average phase during incorrect trials.
source: For the principal cells coherent to beta15-35 Hz during Correct Trials Only, the preferred phase during correct trials was anti-correlated to the average phase during incorrect trials (Rbeta-correct = -0.35, p=0.0027)
evidence: Statistical analysis of phase correlations for beta coherent principal cells.

claim: The principal cells coherent to low gamma35-55 Hz during Correct Trials Only exhibited similar phases across correct and incorrect trials.
source: In contrast, the principal cells coherent to low gamma35-55 Hz during Correct Trials Only exhibited similar phases across correct and incorrect trials (Rlow gamma-correct = 0.35, p=0.0006)
evidence: Statistical analysis of phase correlations for low gamma coherent principal cells.

claim: The distribution of interneurons across the fifteen rhythmic categories was significantly different during correct and incorrect trial types.
source: The distribution of interneurons across the fifteen rhythmic categories was significantly different during correct and incorrect trial types (χ2correct v incorrect (14, N=234) = 52.46, p<0.00001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of interneuron distributions across trial types.

claim: The majority of principal cells exhibited coherence to a single rhythmic circuit during both correct and incorrect trial types.
source: The majority of principal cells exhibited coherence to a single rhythmic circuit during both correct and incorrect trial types.
evidence: This is stated as a finding regarding principal cell engagement patterns.

claim: There were no significant differences in the correlations values obtained for any pair of rhythms for the subpopulation of interneurons that were coherent to all four rhythms.
source: There were no significant differences in the correlations values obtained for any pair of rhythms for the subpopulation of interneurons that were coherent to all four rhythms (one-way repeated measures ANOVA, N=53, d.f. = 5, F= 1.59, p=0.1648).
evidence: Statistical analysis of coherence correlations across rhythms.

claim: Theta4-12 Hz and beta15-35 Hz amplitudes, as well as beta15-35H and low gamma35-55 Hz amplitudes were more correlated than most other pairs of frequencies.
source: In contrast, theta4-12 Hz and beta15-35 Hz amplitudes, as well as beta15-35H and low gamma35-55 Hz amplitudes were more correlated than most other pairs of frequencies (Tukey's Honest Significant Difference test, ptheta-beta v theta-low gamma < 0.00001, ptheta-beta v theta-high gamma < 0.00001, ptheta-beta v beta-low gamma = 0.248, ptheta-beta v beta-high gamma = 0.020, pbeta-low gamma v beta-high gamma = 0.676; pbeta-low gamma v theta-low gamma < 0.00001, pbeta-low gamma v theta-high gamma < 0.00001, pbeta-low gamma v beta-high gamma < 0.00001, pbeta-low gamma v low gamma-high gamma = 0.003).
evidence: Statistical analysis of amplitude correlations between frequency pairs.

claim: Principal cells in the hippocampus have been shown to exhibit activity that is highly selective to spatial positions, sensory stimuli, and the co-occurrence of these features during associative memory tasks.
source: Principal cells in the hippocampus have been shown to exhibit activity that is highly selective to spatial positions, sensory stimuli, and the co-occurrence of these features during associative memory tasks (Figure 6a,b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1–4) (Komorowski et al., 2009; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Eichenbaum et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and references to figures.

claim: Beta15-35 Hz rhythmic circuits may be particularly selective for processing odor-position information, which is critical for successful task performance.
source: Moreover, beta15-35 Hz rhythmic circuits may be particularly selective for processing odor-position information, which is critical for successful task performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the information analysis results.

claim: Task-related processing coincided with the engagement of interneurons into local rhythmic circuits.
source: We found that task-related processing coincided with the engagement of interneurons into local rhythmic circuits.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings in the Discussion.

claim: Engagement arises from a reorganization of spike timing with respect to each rhythm during task-related processing, and not from enhanced participation through differences in overall firing rate between correct and incorrect trials.
source: These measures demonstrated that engagement arises from a reorganization of spike timing with respect to each rhythm during task-related processing (Figure 2a, Figure 3a and b), and not from enhanced participation through differences in overall firing rate between correct and incorrect trials (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coherence and firing rate results with references to figures.

claim: The relationship between task performance and interneuron engagement differed across the four frequency ranges examined.
source: Importantly, the relationship between task performance and interneuron engagement differed across the four frequency ranges examined, suggesting that coordination within each rhythm may have a differential contribution to task-related processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential engagement patterns across rhythms.

claim: Task-related processing consistently recruits interneurons into beta15-35 Hz rhythmic circuits.
source: In contrast, interneurons that exhibited significant spike-phase coherence to beta15-35 Hz were coherent almost exclusively during correct trials, suggesting that task-related processing consistently recruits interneurons into beta15-35 Hz rhythmic circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the beta coherence results.

claim: Each rhythm contributes uniquely to the orchestration of spike timing in the service of task-related processing.
source: As the proportions of cells coherent during Correct Trials Only and All Trials differ across the four rhythms, we can surmise that each rhythm contributes uniquely to the orchestration of spike timing in the service of task-related processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential coherence patterns across rhythms.

claim: Task-related processing more consistently recruits principal cell activity in beta15-35 Hz, low gamma35-55 Hz, and high gamma65-90 Hz rhythmic circuits than in theta4-12 Hz rhythmic circuits.
source: Beta15-35 Hz, low gamma35-55 Hz, and high gamma65-90 Hz coherent principal cells exhibited this preferential coherence during Correct Trials Only more often than theta4-12 Hz coherent principal cells, which consisted of a larger proportion of cells that were coherent irrespective of trial outcome. Though this difference is less pronounced in theta rhythmic principal cells than theta rhythmic interneurons, it nonetheless suggests that task-related processing more consistently recruits principal cell activity in beta15-35 Hz, low gamma35-55 Hz, and high gamma65-90 Hz rhythmic circuits than in theta4-12 Hz rhythmic circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the principal cell coherence patterns.

claim: There is an organization of principal cell spike timing that is unique to correct trials.
source: The strength of principal cell coherence to each rhythm was also greater during correct trials than during incorrect trials (Figure 4a and b), suggesting that there is an organization of principal cell spike timing that is unique to correct trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coherence strength differences.

claim: There are features of engagement in low gamma35-55 Hz rhythmic circuits that are independent of trial outcome.
source: In contrast, the principal cells coherent to low gamma35-55 Hz during Correct Trials Only exhibited similar phases across correct and incorrect trials, suggesting that there are features of engagement in low gamma35-55 Hz rhythmic circuits that are independent of trial outcome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase preference results for low gamma coherent principal cells.

claim: Each rhythmic circuit uniquely engages interneurons in processing states that differentially contribute to task performance.
source: Moreover, the heterogeneity across rhythms indicates that each rhythmic circuit uniquely engages interneurons in processing states that differentially contribute to task performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the heterogeneity in interneuron engagement patterns.

claim: Interneuron engagement in multiple rhythmic circuits is important for task-related processing.
source: Indeed, interneuron spike-phase coherence to multiple rhythms might be a signature of correct performance, whereas interneuron engagement in a single rhythm is more often observed during incorrect trials. This result indicates that the flexible engagement of the interneuron population in multiple rhythmic circuits is important for task-related processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the multi-rhythm engagement patterns.

claim: Theta4-12 Hz, beta15-35 Hz, low gamma35-55 Hz and high gamma65-90 Hz reflect functionally distinct processing states.
source: In contrast, larger numbers of principal cells were preferentially coherent to only one rhythm (Figure 5b), providing evidence that theta4-12 Hz, beta15-35 Hz, low gamma35-55 Hz and high gamma65-90 Hz reflect functionally distinct processing states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the single-rhythm engagement pattern in principal cells.

claim: Principal cells can often participate in segregated rhythmic circuits with separable functions.
source: This result suggests that principal cells can often participate in segregated rhythmic circuits with separable functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the principal cell engagement patterns.

claim: Engagement in multiple rhythmic circuits appears more related to task performance in the interneuron population.
source: Moreover, as many principal cells were engaged in single rhythmic circuits during correct and incorrect trials, engagement in multiple rhythmic circuits appears more related to task performance in the interneuron population.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing interneuron and principal cell engagement patterns.

claim: Interneurons and principal cells interact with the surrounding rhythmic circuits in markedly different ways.
source: These dramatically different profiles of engagement between interneurons and principal cells indicate that each group interacts with the surrounding rhythmic circuits in markedly different ways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences between cell types.

claim: Beta15-35 Hz coherent interneurons may be co-modulated by theta4-12 Hz and low gamma35-55 Hz rhythmic circuits.
source: Specifically, beta15-35 Hz amplitude was often correlated with theta4-12 Hz and low gamma35-55 Hz amplitude, revealing a potential for beta15-35 Hz coherent interneurons to be co-modulated by theta4-12 Hz and low gamma35-55 Hz rhythmic circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amplitude correlation results.

claim: Interneuron engagement in theta4-12 Hz and low gamma35-55 Hz rhythmic circuits may occur at different time points during the nose poke interval.
source: Interestingly, theta15-35 Hz amplitude was often anti-correlated with low gamma35-55 Hz amplitude, suggesting that interneuron engagement in theta4-12 Hz and low gamma35-55 Hz rhythmic circuits may occur at different time points during the nose poke interval.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anti-correlation between theta and low gamma amplitudes.

claim: There is some consistency in the organization of interneuron activity within each of the four rhythms that can include both co-modulation within some rhythmic circuits and temporally segregated entrainment in others.
source: These coordinated dynamics among specific pairs of rhythms suggest that there is some consistency in the organization of interneuron activity within each of the four rhythms that can include both co-modulation within some rhythmic circuits and temporally segregated entrainment in others.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amplitude correlation patterns.

claim: The engagement of principal cells in single rhythmic circuits may provide a mechanism for the hippocampus to simultaneously engage subpopulations of cells in distinct task-relevant processes.
source: The engagement of principal cells in single rhythmic circuits may provide a mechanism for the hippocampus to simultaneously engage subpopulations of cells in distinct task-relevant processes.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the single-rhythm engagement pattern.

claim: Subpopulations of principal cells become differentially engaged in their surrounding rhythmic circuits as a consequence of subtle differences in innervation from heterogeneous afferents or differences in the narrow-band intrinsic resonance of CA1 principal cells.
source: It is possible that subpopulations of principal cells become differentially engaged in their surrounding rhythmic circuits as a consequence of subtle differences in innervation from heterogeneous afferents or differences in the narrow-band intrinsic resonance of CA1 principal cells (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996; Stark et al., 2013.).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Task-related increases in coherence could facilitate the effective communication of subpopulations of CA1 neurons with specific downstream targets that exhibit similar resonance.
source: Task-related increases in coherence could then facilitate the effective communication of subpopulations of CA1 neurons with specific downstream targets that exhibit similar resonance.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism for how coherence might facilitate communication.

claim: The ability of a single network to process information at multiple different frequencies creates an opportunity for multiplexing through frequency division and the selective readout of signals that are segregated into different frequency bands.
source: The ability of a single network to process information at multiple different frequencies thus creates an opportunity for multiplexing through frequency division and the selective readout of signals that are segregated into different frequency bands (Akam and Kullmann, 2014.).
evidence: This is a proposed functional interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Each rhythm reflects a distinct circuit process.
source: We demonstrate that the principal cells coherent to each rhythm can contribute task-relevant information at different time intervals during the odor-sampling epoch (Figure 6c–e), providing further evidence that each rhythm reflects a distinct circuit process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the information analysis results.

claim: Theta4-12 Hz coherent principal cells have a dissociable contribution to the processing of odor information.
source: Information for odors increased earlier in theta4-12 Hz coherent principal cells than in low gamma35-55 Hz and high gamma65-90 Hz coherent principal cells, indicating that theta4-12 Hz coherent principal cells have a dissociable contribution to the processing of odor information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal differences in information increases.

claim: Beta15-35 Hz rhythmic circuits might be uniquely processing information that is critical for successful utilization of associative memory.
source: Coupled with the fact that interneurons are coherent to beta15-35 Hz primarily during correct trials (Figure 2a), our results strongly suggest that beta15-35 Hz rhythmic circuits might be uniquely processing information that is critical for successful utilization of associative memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining multiple findings.

claim: The selective entrainment of the interneuron population to beta15-25 Hz during correct trials could reflect the receipt of rhythmic input from an upstream structure that engages neurons in the hippocampus.
source: The selective entrainment of the interneuron population to beta15-25 Hz during correct trials (Figure 2a) could reflect the receipt of rhythmic input from an upstream structure that engages neurons in the hippocampus (Figure 4d, mechanism 1).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for beta rhythm generation.

claim: Coherence between the CA1 and the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) parallels the onset of learning in an olfactory discrimination task and the development of task-selective ensemble activity.
source: This hypothesis is supported by recent studies suggesting that coherence between the CA1 and the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) parallels the onset of learning in an olfactory discrimination task and the development of task-selective ensemble activity (Igarashi et al., 2014; Rangel and Eichenbaum, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The LEC has been shown to be important for the processing of multi-modal object information.
source: As the LEC has been shown to be important for the processing of multi-modal object information (Young et al., 1997; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011), communication between LEC and hippocampus could be critical for the association of odors with their reward contingencies.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Beta oscillations in the dentate gyrus are likely driven by perforant path input.
source: In addition, a recent study that used current source density analysis to reveal the location of current sources and sinks corresponding to beta oscillations in the dentate gyrus found that beta oscillations in this structure are likely driven by perforant path input (Rangel et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Beta oscillatory dynamics in the CA1 may be the product of entrainment by an upstream cortical afferent.
source: It is thus possible that beta oscillatory dynamics in the CA1 are the product of entrainment by an upstream cortical afferent.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior findings.

claim: The hippocampus may locally generate a beta15-25 Hz rhythm when engaged by specific afferents.
source: As an alternative to inheriting beta15-25 Hz rhythmicity from upstream structures, it is also possible that the hippocampus locally generates a beta15-25 Hz rhythm when engaged by specific afferents (Figure 4d, mechanism 2).
evidence: This is a proposed alternative mechanism for beta rhythm generation.

claim: The beta15-25 Hz rhythm could reflect the broad coordination of activity across disparate neural networks.
source: As a third possibility, the beta15-25 Hz rhythm could reflect the broad coordination of activity across disparate neural networks (Kopell et al., 2000; Bibbig et al., 2002; Pinto et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a proposed third mechanism supported by citations.

claim: The hippocampus is one of many structures that engage in beta rhythmic processing during the presentation of meaningful cues.
source: The hippocampus is just one of many structures that engage in beta rhythmic processing during the presentation of meaningful cues (Igarashi et al., 2014; Kay and Freeman, 1998; Rangel et al., 2015; Quinn et al., 2010; Buschman et al., 2012; Leventhal, 2012; Tingley et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Rhythmic synchronization of a distributed network through a central rhythm generator could enable information processing as a coordinated unit.
source: Rhythmic synchronization of this distributed network through a central rhythm generator could then enable information processing as a coordinated unit (Figure 4d, mechanism 3).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism for coordinated network processing.

claim: Interneuron and principal cell coherence have distinct relationships to task performance.
source: We found two major differences in the rhythmic organization of CA1 interneuron and principal cell activity during a memory task. First, interneuron and principal cell coherence have distinct relationships to task performance.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a major finding.

claim: Interneurons, unlike principal cells, are often flexibly engaged in multiple rhythms.
source: Second, we show that interneurons, unlike principal cells, are often flexibly engaged in multiple rhythms.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a major finding.

claim: Different rhythms make unique contributions to information processing within the hippocampus.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that different rhythms make unique contributions to information processing within the hippocampus, and changes in the rhythmic profile reflect dynamic coordination of its cell activity.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Six male Long-Evans rats were used as subjects in the study.
source: Subjects were six male Long-Evans rats (Charles River Laboratories) housed individually and maintained on a 12-hr light/dark cycle.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: All neural recordings were performed during the light cycle.
source: All neural recordings were performed during the light cycle.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the recordings.

claim: Rats were food and water restricted, and maintained at a weight of at least 85–90% of ad libitum body weight.
source: Rats were food and water restricted, and maintained at a weight of at least 85–90% of ad libitum body weight.
evidence: This describes the maintenance conditions for the rats.

claim: Each hyperdrive contained 24 microdrives, each with an independently drivable tetrode.
source: Following training, each rat was surgically implanted with a hyperdrive containing 24 microdrives, each with an independently drivable tetrode.
evidence: This describes the recording device implanted in the rats.

claim: Each tetrode was composed of four strands of 0.0005" (12 µm) Nickel-Chrome wire, gold-plated to reduce impedance to 200–250 kOhms at 1000 Hz.
source: Each tetrode was composed of four strands of 0.0005" (12 µm) Nickel-Chrome wire (Sandvik, Stockholm, Sweden), gold-plated to reduce impedance to 200–250 kOhms at 1000 Hz.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the tetrodes.

claim: The implant site was located over the right dorsal hippocampus (A/P = -4.0 mm; M/L = 2.2 mm).
source: The implant site was located over the right dorsal hippocampus (A/P = -4.0 mm; M/L = 2.2 mm), and tetrodes were turned down an initial 1.6 mm into the brain immediately following surgery.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of the implant.

claim: Tetrodes were progressively lowered over the training period (6–7 weeks) to the principal cell layer of CA1 (D/V = ~1.9 mm).
source: After rats received a two-week recovery period, tetrodes were progressively lowered over the training period (6–7 weeks) to the principal cell layer of CA1 (D/V = ~1.9 mm).
evidence: This describes the procedure for positioning the tetrodes.

claim: Signals were amplified by a preamplifier 20x and amplified again to 4,000–6,000x.
source: Signals were amplified by a preamplifier 20x and amplified again to 4,000–6,000x (Plexon, Dallas, TX), with a band-pass filter of 400–8,000 Hz to digitally isolate spikes (OmniPlex, Plexon).
evidence: This describes the signal amplification parameters.

claim: Local field potentials (LFPs) were digitally isolated with a band-pass filter from 1–400 Hz.
source: Local field potentials (LFPs) were digitally isolated with a band-pass filter from 1–400 Hz.
evidence: This describes the filtering parameters for LFP recordings.

claim: Only sessions in which the rats performed at greater than 75% accuracy were used in analysis.
source: Only sessions in which the rats performed at greater than 75% accuracy were used in analysis.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for data analysis.

claim: Interneurons exhibited mean firing rates of at least 5 Hz, a mean width at half-max less than 150 μs, and a mean peak to trough waveform width less than 350 μs.
source: Interneurons exhibited mean firing rates of at least 5 Hz, a mean width at half-max less than 150 μs, and a mean peak to trough waveform width less than 350 μs, while principal cells exhibited mean firing rates of less than 3 Hz with wider waveforms (Stark et al., 2013; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Bartho, 2004).
evidence: This describes the criteria for classifying interneurons, supported by citations.

claim: Principal cells exhibited mean firing rates of less than 3 Hz with wider waveforms.
source: Interneurons exhibited mean firing rates of at least 5 Hz, a mean width at half-max less than 150 μs, and a mean peak to trough waveform width less than 350 μs, while principal cells exhibited mean firing rates of less than 3 Hz with wider waveforms (Stark et al., 2013; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Bartho, 2004).
evidence: This describes the criteria for classifying principal cells, supported by citations.
